articles.title: 'I'm not broken...': At 21, he survived burns on 85% of his body after a gas explosion, years later he prepares school lunches for hundreds of students while building his dream life
articles.summary: At 21, Joey Brown survived a gas explosion that left burns across 85% of his body, beginning a long and painful journey of surgeries, rehabilitation and
articles.body: At 21, Joey Brown survived a gas explosion that left burns across 85% of his body, beginning a long and painful journey of surgeries, rehabilitation and learning to perform everyday tasks again. Decades later, he is rebuilding his life in a Georgia high school cafeteria, where he helps care for hundreds of students and has found a community that believes in him. Now, as he looks towards owning a home and welcoming a beagle named Snoopy, Brown says he no longer sees himself as a broken man.A report published by CBS Atlanta documented how Brown, who works at Central High School in Carrollton, Georgia, found renewed purpose through employment and the support of his church. The Georgia Vocational Rehabilitation Agency (GVRA), which helped him secure the job, had previously detailed the long road that brought him back into the workforce.A gas explosion changed his life foreverIn 1988, Brown had recently moved out of his parents’ home and was sharing an apartment with his brother in Winter Garden, Florida. According to GVRA, he was watching an Atlanta Braves baseball game when he lit a cigarette. The flame ignited fumes from a gas leak, triggering an explosion that knocked him unconscious. When Brown regained consciousness in the apartment complex’s parking lot, a police officer was standing over him and help was on the way. He was airlifted to a hospital in Orlando, where doctors determined that he had sustained severe burns across 85% of his body.The injuries would change nearly every aspect of his life. Brown eventually lost his left arm at the elbow and was left with four fingers on his right hand. His recovery involved repeated operations and a prolonged hospital stay. “I’ve had probably 30 to 50 surgeries over the years,” Brown told CBS Atlanta. “I was in the hospital for two and a half years. I had to learn how to walk again and feed myself again.”The physical injuries were only part of the struggle. For years, Brown found it difficult to face the outside world, conscious of the scars that made strangers stare at him. “For a long time, I hid from the world. And because of my burns and scars, people would stare at me. But it doesn’t bother me no more,” he told CBS Atlanta.Finding a family when he needed oneBrown’s journey back to independence was not something he managed alone. His faith and his involvement with Midway Church in Villa Rica, Georgia, helped him build relationships and find a sense of belonging. He became a greeter at the church, where his willingness to encourage others made him an important presence in the community. Members came to know him not simply as a man who had survived a devastating accident, but as someone who continued to offer kindness despite his own difficulties.“He is a great, great encourager to many, many people, and they depend on that,” Kay Thompson of Midway Church told CBS Atlanta. Brown said the relationships he developed at church helped fill a deeply felt absence in his life.“I prayed a long time for my own family, and Jesus showed me families every week to come and see me and visit me,” he said. It was through this community that Brown began working towards another milestone: finding a permanent job and becoming more independent.The people who helped him find workAccording to GVRA, Brown first approached the agency for assistance in 2020, but his case did not progress at that time. With encouragement from church member Gerry Herlugson, he reapplied in March 2024 and began receiving vocational rehabilitation services. The agency connected him with Wiregrass Resource Group, a supported-employment organisation, where Kehli Pope became his job coach. Together, they worked towards finding an employer willing to give Brown an opportunity.One unexpected obstacle was the fingerprint-based background check required for school employment. Brown no longer had fingerprints because of his injuries. Pope contacted the school system and helped secure acceptance of a doctor’s note explaining his condition.She also helped him adjust to his responsibilities in the cafeteria, drawing on skills he had already developed while washing dishes at church. “He washes dishes like a pro,” Pope told GVRA.Brown’s work at Central High School includes operating the commercial dishwasher, disposing of rubbish and helping clean his coworkers’ workstations. After the school year ended in May 2026, he also took a position as an aide in the district’s summer meal programme. His coworkers have welcomed him as one of their own. Beana Nolley, who works alongside him, told CBS Atlanta that Brown brings energy and warmth to the kitchen. “Mr. Joey lights up our kitchen,” she said.Nolley also described how students notice Brown working despite having one arm, using his example to encourage them to believe in their own abilities. For Brown, the job has brought something he had struggled to find after years of uncertainty: a reason to look forward to the next day.“It makes me look forward to tomorrow because I didn’t have nothing to look forward to and give myself hope. And now I got hope from having a job again,” he told CBS Atlanta.A home of his own and a beagle named SnoopyWith employment providing greater stability, Brown has begun looking beyond simply getting through each day. His next goal is to own a home, where he can live more independently and welcome a dog of his own. GVRA reported in July that Brown had been living with his sister for 14 years and hoped to purchase his first home by December 2026. He has been saving towards that goal, while Herlugson has organised a separate fundraiser to help with the down payment.Brown already knows what he wants to call his future companion. “I want to be in my own home by December, so I can celebrate Christmas with my new puppy. My puppy is a beagle. I have decided to name him Snoopy,” he told GVRA.Church members have offered to contribute their time, labour and, in some cases, building materials to help him achieve his dream. Herlugson told CBS Atlanta that the project had become a shared goal for the community.After years in which his injuries and scars shaped how he saw himself, Brown is now looking towards a future defined by his own choices. “I was a broken man now, and I’m not broken no more,” he told CBS Atlanta.For Brown, the dream is not simply about a house or a puppy. It is about the independence, belonging and everyday happiness he spent years trying to regain, and the people who helped him believe those things were still possible.You use AI every day. articles.title: Queen Elizabeth’s Sandringham estate planted more than 5,000 trees a year and created 10 wetlands as part of its conservation work
articles.summary: Sandringham is best known as the Norfolk country estate closely associated with the British royal family, but its land has also been managed with wildlife
articles.body: Sandringham is best known as the Norfolk country estate closely associated with the British royal family, but its land has also been managed with wildlife and long-term conservation in mind. As reported by the Royal Households of the United Kingdom, more than 5,000 trees are planted there each year, alongside several miles of hedges, while 10 wetland areas have been created to provide habitats for wildlife. These efforts formed part of a wider approach to maintaining the estate for future generations, a principle that Prince Philip took a personal interest in during his lifetime. Although responsibility for running Sandringham has since passed to King Charles III, the conservation practices established under his father remain part of its management.How Prince Philip introduced wildlife conservation measures at SandringhamPrince Philip assumed responsibility for managing Sandringham at the beginning of Queen Elizabeth II’s reign in 1952. The estate was privately owned by the monarch rather than held as part of the Crown Estate, and its management involved balancing agricultural activity with the protection of its natural environment.Philip took an active interest in how the land was maintained, with conservation forming part of his wider approach to the royal family's private estates. At Sandringham, this included allocating resources to improve habitats for wildlife, particularly birds that nest on the ground. The estate also established more than 100 miles of field margins, strips of land around cultivated fields that can provide shelter, food and nesting opportunities for different species.Reportedly, the annual planting of more than 5,000 trees, together with several miles of new hedges, helped maintain and extend the estate's network of wooded areas and vegetation.Sandringham’s 10 wetlands add new habitats for wildlifeThe creation of 10 wetland areas added another element to Sandringham's conservation programme. Wetlands provide conditions that can support a range of plants, insects, birds and other animals, depending on their size, water levels and surrounding vegetation. Their presence also adds habitat variety to a landscape that includes farmland, woodland and managed gardens.The estate's approach does not rely on planting trees alone. Farming practices are adapted to encourage different forms of wildlife, allowing agricultural land to serve purposes beyond food production. Field margins, hedgerows and wetland areas can each contribute to this work, offering different conditions for species to feed, shelter and reproduce.Waste recycling and long-term land management at SandringhamEnvironmental management at Sandringham also extends to the handling of everyday waste. Food waste, glass, metals, plastic, cardboard and paper are recycled as part of the estate's operations. These measures sit alongside its woodland, hedgerow and wetland projects, covering both the management of the land and the resources used to run the property.The estate remains a working landscape, meaning conservation has to take place alongside farming and other activities. Practices intended to encourage wildlife are therefore incorporated into the management of the land rather than treated as separate from its agricultural use.The annual tree planting figure is particularly significant in this context because it represents recurring work rather than a single restoration project.King Charles III took over Sandringham’s management in 2017King Charles III assumed responsibility for running Sandringham in 2017, continuing the management approach developed during Prince Philip's involvement. The transition marked a change in who oversaw the estate, while conservation remained among the principles guiding its operations.Sandringham is one of several royal properties where Philip took a close interest in environmental management. His involvement also extended to Balmoral in Scotland and Windsor's Great and Home Parks, where his projects included woodland regeneration, tree planting and changes to the management of gardens and buildings.A small area was enclosed for an initial regeneration trial in the early 1970s, followed by a larger section in 1979. The protected area expanded again in 1992, eventually covering about 300 hectares. Further areas were enclosed in later years, including in 2016.His work across the estates varied according to the landscape, from protecting woodland to improving habitats and developing gardens.You use AI every day. articles.title: Israel elections: Anti-Netanyahu bloc weighs direct PM election bill to break political deadlock
articles.summary: Israel's opposition bloc is considering legislation to introduce direct elections for prime minister in a bid to break the political deadlock following
articles.body: Israel's opposition bloc is considering legislation to introduce direct elections for prime minister in a bid to break the political deadlock following Tuesday's inconclusive election and potentially form a minority government without relying on Arab parties, according to The Times of Israel.The proposal would allow voters to elect the prime minister separately from the government, potentially enabling a candidate who wins the direct contest to form a minority administration without securing a majority in the 120-member Knesset.Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition secured a majority in Tuesday's election, leaving both sides struggling to find a viable arrangement to form the next government.Netanyahu had also pushed a similar proposal following the inconclusive March 2021 election, when his efforts to assemble a governing coalition had stalled.However, implementing the proposed system would require an amendment to Israel's Basic Law: The Government, which currently requires a prospective government to secure a vote of confidence in the Knesset before being sworn in. The amendment would need the support of at least 61 lawmakers, The Times of Israel reported.Protests planned in support of Jewish-Arab coalitionMeanwhile, demonstrations are expected across Israel on Saturday evening, with organisers calling for the opposition's so-called change bloc to form a government based on Jewish-Arab cooperation.According to The Times of Israel, the Standing Together group has announced rallies at 7:30 pm at Tel Aviv's Habima Square, Jerusalem's Paris Square, as well as in Beersheba, Haifa and Tayibe.The demonstrations aim to press opposition leaders to recognise the bloc's electoral victory and form a government in partnership with Arab parties.Tuesday's election saw the opposition secure 67 seats against 53 for the coalition. However, the opposition's tally includes 48 seats won by Zionist parties and 19 secured by Arab non-Zionist parties, whose support Jewish opposition leaders had previously been reluctant to accept."Protesters are demanding that the bloc's leaders recognise their victory and form a government based on Jewish-Arab partnership," the organisers said."The Jewish-Arab majority that voted for change must also be reflected in the next government. Now is not the time to abandon our partnership, but to turn it into a political force that changes reality. Arab votes are worth exactly as much as Jewish votes, and Arab citizens must be full partners in shaping the country's future," they added.The rallies come as opposition parties continue to explore possible governing arrangements, with cooperation with Arab parties emerging as a key hurdle in their efforts to keep Netanyahu out of power.The final official election results will be submitted to Israeli President Isaac Herzog on November 4, following checks into possible errors and other inquiries. The newly elected Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on November 10.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav on Saturday dismissed Union home minister Amit Shah's claim that the BJP was firmly entrenched in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav on Saturday dismissed Union home minister Amit Shah's claim that the BJP was firmly entrenched in Uttar Pradesh, questioning him over crimes against women and Dalits in the state. Party MP Awadhesh Prasad also hit back at Shah's "Angad's foot" remark, saying the BJP's political footing had "already been uprooted".According to PTI, Akhilesh made the remarks while responding to Shah's assertion that the BJP government in Uttar Pradesh was firmly established and could not be dislodged."Home minister should look into why women face so much injustice in Uttar Pradesh, why the state witnesses so many murders and why people from the Dalit community are among the worst affected," Akhilesh said.He questioned the BJP's claims of political stability in the state, shifting the focus to the government's record on law and order and the treatment of women and Dalits.Reacting to Shah's claim that the BJP government in Uttar Pradesh was firmly entrenched, Samajwadi Party MP Awadhesh Prasad said the party had already lost ground in the state.Responding to Shah's comparison of the BJP's position to "Angad's foot", Awadhesh said, "The foot has already been uprooted."Awadhesh said the BJP had failed to retain several seats in the recent Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council elections despite making every effort. He cited the party's defeats in Varanasi, Lucknow and Agra, and also referred to its loss in Prayagraj, a prominent educational centre.He also pointed to the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, saying the BJP had failed to achieve its target of winning all 80 seats in Uttar Pradesh. The SP won 37 seats, while the Congress secured six, taking the INDIA bloc's tally to 43 seats in the state.Shah made the remarks on Friday while addressing the BJP's state working committee meeting at the Dr Ram Manohar Lohia National Law University auditorium in Lucknow.The meeting was attended by Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath, Deputy Chief Ministers Keshav Prasad Maurya and Brajesh Pathak, and other senior BJP leaders. Shah expressed confidence that the BJP would return to power in the 2027 Assembly elections, comparing the party's position in Uttar Pradesh to "Angad's foot" and saying nobody could dislodge it.He also announced that the BJP would implement the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in Uttar Pradesh if voted back to power. Targeting the Samajwadi Party over the Ram temple issue, Shah referred to the October 30, 1990, police firing on kar sevaks in Ayodhya and accused the SP of ordering firing on Ram devotees, while asserting that the BJP had built the Ram temple.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2014, the 5.5-carat Ocean Dream sold for about $8.5 million; in May 2026 the same blue-green diamond, the largest of its kind known, sold at Christie’s Geneva for $17.3 million, roughly double
articles.summary: Diamonds, formed deep within the Earth, have become the ultimate symbols of luxury, wealth and timeless beauty.
articles.body: Diamonds, formed deep within the Earth, have become the ultimate symbols of luxury, wealth and timeless beauty. But some are so rare that their value goes far beyond their size and sparkle. Diamonds are not just another gemstone; historically and socially, they have become a greater part of human civilisation. From India's Kohinoor and France's Regent Diamond to literally every engagement ring, the preciousness of these stones has overlapped with the preciousness of our moments.One such gemstone is the Ocean Dream, a 5.50-carat natural blue-green diamond that recently sold for $17.3 million at Christie's Geneva auction in May 2026. What makes the sale particularly interesting is that the same diamond had also appeared at an auction 12 years earlier, when it fetched approximately $8.5 million. In other words, its dollar-denominated auction price has nearly doubled in just over a decade, making it one of the most remarkable sales in the coloured diamond market.What makes the Ocean Dream diamond so rare?The Ocean Dream is not an ordinary blue diamond. According to Christie's, the international auction house that auctioned the diamond in Geneva, it is classified as a Fancy Vivid Blue-Green diamond. It is considered the largest known diamond in its particular colour category. The gemstone weighs 5.50 carats and has a triangular cut, with a clarity grade of SI1. Its distinctive colour and relatively large size make it especially unusual in the world of natural coloured diamonds.The finished diamond weighs less than half of its original rough form. The stone also has an interesting history. Its original rough form weighed 11.70 carats and was discovered in Central Africa during the 1990s. It was subsequently cut and polished into the triangular gemstone that collectors recognise today, reducing it to less than half of its original weight.How did the diamond get its unusual blue-green colour?While most people associate diamonds with being glassy and colourless, they can naturally occur in several shades, including pink, yellow, blue, green and red. These colours develop because of differences in the diamond's internal structure and the presence of certain impurities or structural changes that affect how it absorbs and reflects light.In the case of the Ocean Dream, its unusual blue-green colour is due to exposure to natural radiation. As radiation interacts with a diamond's crystal structure over geological periods, it can displace carbon atoms and create defects known as colour centres. These defects change the way light passes through the gemstone, producing vibrant colours.Green diamonds are particularly interesting because natural radiation often affects only the outer layers of a stone. A strongly coloured diamond that retains its unusual appearance after cutting and polishing is therefore exceptionally rare. The Ocean Dream's vivid blue-green appearance is what makes it so distinctive among known natural-coloured diamonds.From a museum exhibition to a multimillion-dollar auctionThe Ocean Dream's history is not limited to auction rooms. In 2003, it was displayed at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in Washington, DC, as part of an exhibition titled The Splendour of Diamonds. The exhibition was extraordinary in itself, as it brought together seven diamonds from different parts of the world, showcasing the remarkable range of colours and brilliance that natural diamonds can possess.The collection included the De Beers Millennium Star, the Steinmetz Pink, the Heart of Eternity and the Pumpkin Diamond, among other famous gemstones. The Ocean Dream stood out for its unusual blue-green colour, which remains exceptionally uncommon even among fancy coloured diamonds.Its previous auction appearance was in May 2014, when it sold at Christie's Geneva for CHF 7.7 million, equivalent to approximately $8.5 million at the time. When it returned to the same auction house in May 2026, it fetched CHF 13.56 million, or approximately $17.3 million. The final price also exceeded its presale estimate of CHF 7 million to CHF 10 million.Why are rare coloured diamonds so expensive?You might think the value of diamonds is determined by their carat weight alone. But that is not entirely true. Though weight plays a major role in determining their value, colour, cut and natural origin all play an important role, particularly in the case of fancy coloured diamonds. Unlike colourless diamonds, where the absence of colour is generally desirable, coloured diamonds are valued for the strength and rarity of their natural hues.The Ocean Dream brings together a naturally occurring royal hue, vivid saturation, a documented history and, most importantly, a remarkable size for a blue-green diamond.Perhaps that is what makes diamonds so fascinating. They are formed in the depths of the Earth, far removed from human civilisation, and yet we have spent centuries giving them meaning, turning them into symbols of love, power, wealth and permanence. The Ocean Dream is another reminder of how nature can create something extraordinary without ever intending it to be precious. It is only when we discover these wonders that we begin to understand just how much beauty exists beyond our making.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: State Department accuses politicians of endangering Afrikaner lives after gruesome farm attacks
articles.summary: The State Department accused South African politicians of endangering Afrikaners' lives after a farmer was allegedly tortured and a woman beaten to death.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The State Department has hit out strongly against South Africa and some of its politicians, accusing them of putting their people’s lives at risk following two attacks on White farmers believed to be Afrikaners — people of European descent — near Johannesburg. A 50-year-old man was reportedly tortured, and a 55-year-old woman allegedly beaten to death. In exclusive comments to Fox News Digital, a State Department spokesperson said "the lives and property of Afrikaners have been endangered by politicians who incite race-based violence against them." BIDEN-ERA DIRECTIVE FOR DIPLOMATS TO PEDDLE DEI ON FOREIGN GOVERNMENTS SCRAPPED BY STATE DEPARTMENT This is the latest volley from the administration in an increasingly bitter row, which first burst out of the Oval Office last year in a heated exchange between President Donald Trump and South Africa’s President Cyril Ramaphosa, on a range of the country’s policies and issues — including safety concerns for the Afrikaner community. "This month’s attacks were ‘appalling,’ said Ian Cameron, chair of South Africa’s Portfolio Committee on Police and a member of Parliament with the main opposition Democratic Alliance. He detailed the attacks, starting with one involving Donovan Marx, a 50-year-old who was on his farm about 80 miles from Johannesburg. Cameron told Fox News Digital there were reports Marx was shot, stabbed and had his ears cut off, describing the attack as "extraordinary cruelty." He added that in a separate attack in the same North West Province earlier this month, a female farmer, Hannetjie van Zyl, 55, was beaten to death while opening a gate. Eyewitness reports claim she was approached from behind and hit repeatedly over the head with an iron bar. In both attacks, the victims’ vehicles and belongings were reportedly stolen. But the alleged torture of Marx goes beyond straightforward crimes such as burglary, Corné Mulder, leader of the opposition party Freedom Front Plus, told Fox News Digital. "Safety and farm attacks in South Africa remains a huge problem," Mulder said. "Donovan Marx was attacked this week. He's fighting for his life in hospital at the moment. The perpetrators not only attacked him, they tried to castrate him." While both victims were White, there have been no accusations from public figures that the attacks were racially motivated. Cameron claimed the attacks were not isolated, noting he had "personally attended farm-attack scenes where people were tortured with boiling water, burnt with clothing irons and subjected to other horrific abuse." "SAPS [South African Police Service] must put experienced investigators, forensic support and crime intelligence behind these cases," Cameron said. "Nobody should have to accept this level of violence as a normal part of life." The reported torture of farmers is "unthinkable," Mulder said, adding "not one word from the President of South Africa to sympathize, not even acknowledging that this has happened, which is absolutely unbelievable." "We have been pleading with [the] government to prioritize rural crime and farm attacks as a priority crime, they are not prepared to do so," he continued. Fox News Digital reached out to the South African government for comment, but was referred to police, who did not immediately respond. SOUTH AFRICAN EX-POLICE CHIEF GETS TISSUE STUCK ON FOREHEAD WHILE SWEATING DURING CORRUPTION INQUIRY Mulder claims the recent farm attacks were fueled by the South African president’s refusal to heed Trump’s demand last year to stop performances of the song "Kill the Boer, Kill the Farmer." The term "Boer" refers to a South African of Dutch or Huguenot descent, according to Merriam-Webster. Ramaphosa said he could not stop the song being chanted in stadiums by crowds of up to 90,000 because the country’s highest court has said the lyrics are not hate speech. THOUSANDS OF POLICE DEPLOYED ACROSS SOUTH AFRICA AS DEADLY ANTI-IMMIGRATION PROTESTS SPREAD TO MULTIPLE CITIES "As long as [President Ramaphosa] does not stop the incitement to attack farmers with the singing of the song "Kill the Boer," the attacks will continue," Mulder wrote in a statement. "We see the practical reality when these things play out as happened with the last two farm attacks that we've seen." Last month, U.S. Ambassador to South Africa Brent Bozell III told Fox News Digital that Ramaphosa could ban the song despite a court ruling that it did not constitute hate speech. "So, to say, well, you can’t do it because the court said it’s not, you know, that’s poppycock," Bozell said. "If President Ramaphosa, if he wants to, he can do it. It’s just as simple as that." The spokesperson added that Trump has demanded South Africa formally designate rural crime as a priority crime, and "expand alternatives to the Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment ownership requirements, such as equity equivalent investment programs." Regarding farmers, the State Department spokesperson said South African politicians "threaten to confiscate their farms without compensation and support a corrupt, race-based scoring system that discriminates against Afrikaners and other minorities in employment." "The lack of a meaningful response to these requests made clear that the South African government does not want a constructive relationship with the United States and is willing to continue pursuing oppressive policies that disadvantage all South Africans," the spokesperson continued. articles.title: Ancient 'rusty treasure' emerges from river with enough iron to forge 500 swords
articles.summary: Over 500 iron bars pulled from the Danube River in Austria may point to a shipwreck that sank a massive Iron Age cargo over 2,000 years ago, researchers say.
articles.body: Archaeologists have identified Europe's largest known collection of Iron Age iron bars in Austria — raising the possibility that the valuable cargo was lost in a shipwreck on the Danube River more than 2,000 years ago. Workers recovered at least 500 bars, making the collection the largest known Iron Age find of its kind in Europe. The "rusty treasure," as researchers called it in a press release, would have been extremely valuable during the Iron Age, when iron production and trade were expanding across Europe. "Fortunately, the gravel workers [who found the iron bars] reported this find to the Monuments Authority and did not sell them to a scrap dealer," Peter Trebsche, a professor at the University of Innsbruck in Austria, told Fox News Digital. 2,000-YEAR-OLD TREASURE DISCOVERED BENEATH FORMER SPORTS FIELD, BREAKING REGIONAL RECORD The iron bars — which weigh more than a metric ton in total — could have been used to forge roughly 500 swords weighing between 3.3 and 4.4 pounds each, according to the researchers. The research was published earlier this fall by archaeologist Trebsche as well as archaeologist Marion Berranger in the journal Antiquity. The iron bars were originally discovered in 2019 during gravel extraction work in Deinham, Austria. Researchers used radiocarbon dating to determine the age of the iron bars, which likely date to the third or second century B.C. MYSTERY DEEPENS AFTER 2,700-YEAR-OLD BRONZE SWORD EMERGES STANDING UPRIGHT While its intended destination remains unknown, researchers believe the iron may have been forged in Bavaria, Germany, before being transported along the Danube River. The discovery sheds new light on the scale of ancient iron production, which has been difficult to measure because iron objects are often overlooked or difficult to date the researchers said. "Fortunately, the gravel workers reported this find to the Monuments Authority and did not sell them to a scrap dealer." "Therefore, the discovery of numerous double-pointed iron objects during gravel extraction along the River Danube provided a unique opportunity to investigate large-scale prehistoric iron production and trade," the press release said. In a statement, Trebsche called the discovery "nothing short of a minor miracle." DIVERS UNCOVER MYSTERIOUS SHIPWRECK LOADED WITH ANCIENT CARGO LOST FOR 2,400 YEARS He added, "I am sincerely grateful to the finders that [the workers] decided to donate this extraordinary trove to a state museum collection." Trebsche told Fox News Digital the iron bars were found during gravel extraction work in an old, silt-filled channel of the Danube River. He said a shipwreck is the most plausible explanation for how the bars ended up in the river, although no remains of a vessel were found. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "No parts of the ship were recovered, because this section of the Danube poses some dangers to navigation like stone balls and sand banks," Trebsche noted. "In support of this interpretation is also the fact that none of the finds shows signs of intentional destruction, which would be indicative of a ritual offering during the Late Iron Age." He also said the 500-sword figure is only an estimate, as the iron could have been used to make tools or jewelry instead of weapons. "The amount of iron from Deinham is about ten times larger than the largest iron hoard finds of that period," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Trebsche said the most surprising aspect of the discovery was the sheer quantity of iron being transported at once — and the fact that so much was available for a single trade transaction during the Late Iron Age. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "This finding demonstrates the increased capacities of iron production that were reached in the 3rd/2nd century BC in the Danube region," he said. A number of other Iron Age discoveries have been announced across Europe over the past year. Earlier this year, archaeologists uncovered a 2,000-year-old temple in Denmark at a major Iron Age settlement that once served as a regional center of power and wealth. articles.title: Storm set to hit central US on Election Day as key midterm races hang in balance
articles.summary: A storm headed for the central United States on Election Day could affect voter turnout in key races across the region.
articles.body: A storm headed for the central United States on Election Day could affect voter turnout in key races across the region. The beginnings of our storm are just off the West Coast and will cross into the US Saturday night. It will funnel in abundant moisture from the tropical Pacific, setting up a serious flooding threat in the Southwest this weekend before it brings soggy weather to the central states for Election Day. Heavy rain is expected to fall over the Four Corners states of Arizona, New Mexico, Utah and Colorado on Sunday into Monday, and could bring serious flash flooding, before the system marches into the central US by Election Day. Soggy weather is likely for a widespread area on Tuesday, stretching from the Great Plains and Upper Midwest to the Lower Mississippi Valley and western Gulf Coast. Stormy conditions are possible for keys races in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan and Texas. The threat of flooding rain on Tuesday is currently low, but voters traveling to the polls could encounter ponding on roads. Thunderstorms are expected on the storm’s southern side, a few of which could intensify and turn severe from eastern Texas into Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Tennessee. Blustery conditions are also likely throughout a large portion of the impacted states, especially in the Plains. Kansas could see wind gusts between 30 to 40 mph, up to 50 mph in Nebraska. Weather conditions could factor in to voter turnout in those states and for others in the central US who aren’t among the more than 49 million people who have already cast ballots through early voting. Rainfall and other active weather tend to suppress voter turnout while sunshine has the opposite effect, multiple studies have found. Dry weather will likely sandwich the storm along much of the East Coast and in the West. The only exception is coastal areas of the Southeast and northern California where nuisance showers can’t be completely ruled out yet. Across the country though, there will be no need to bundle up to go vote. High temperatures in most of the nation’s eastern half are forecast to be 5 to 20 degrees Fahrenheit above average. Only portions of the the Southwest will have temperatures tilting a bit cooler than average. The breakdown below shows the forecast for some of the key states in the midterms. articles.title: Syria considering entry into Mecca defence pact, says foreign minister
articles.summary: Damascus ‘evaluating’ whether to join the alliance that binds Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
articles.body:
Syria’s government is weighing whether to enter into a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan, the country’s top diplomat says.

“Discussions are currently under way to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Mecca alliance,” Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said at the Manama Dialogue conference in Bahrain on Saturday.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement was signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan in the Saudi city of Mecca in August. It states that an attack on one country is to be considered an attack on all three, and has been compared to the NATO security alliance that binds the United States, Canada and 30 European countries.

Saudi Arabia, under heavy fire from Yemen’s Houthis, is a key backer of Syria’s government led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa, which came to power after the fall of former strongman Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.

Under the Mecca pact, Pakistan and Turkiye have pledged military support to Riyadh as it faces escalating attacks from the Iran-backed group. However, neither Islamabad nor Ankara has yet announced any attacks on the Houthis.

Government officials in Turkiye, where the pact’s ratification process is ongoing , have said any future military support for Riyadh would not include deploying Turkish troops to fight in Yemen or attack the Houthis.

Speaking at the conference in Bahrain, al-Shaibani said Damascus was an “integral” part of regional security and would support any framework aimed at protecting regional stability.

The minister stressed that the region was “in greater need than ever” of developing joint deterrence and defence systems.

He said Syria backs the efforts of Yemen’s Saudi-backed internationally recognised government to restore “sovereignty and stability across its entire territory” as it battles the Houthis, Syrian state media reported.

He also urged all parties to support the unity and sovereignty of states.

Separately, the minister said Israel has carried out more than 1,000 attacks on Syria in less than two years, killing dozens of people.

“How can calls for border control and placing weapons exclusively under state control be justified while Syrian sovereignty is violated and targeted on a daily basis?” he asked.

articles.title: Iran FM says US outreach a ‘positive step’ as delegation in Qatar for talks
articles.summary: Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi tells Al Jazeera Tehran doesn’t rule out attack, is ‘prepared for all scenarios’.
articles.body:
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says a United States effort to open dialogue with Tehran is “a positive step”, but that there are currently no plans for meetings with US officials regarding the eight-month-old war.

Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had studied a letter sent by US Vice President JD Vance in high-level meetings, and set out Tehran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which he said would pave the way for renewed negotiations with Washington.

He added that an Iranian delegation has travelled to Doha, a day after Qatari mediators were in Tehran in an apparent bid to negotiate a revival of the US-Iran ceasefire. Araghchi said one of his aides is in Qatar to continue consultations.

“The American side’s attempt to open the door to dialogue and understanding more broadly is a positive step,” the foreign minister told Al Jazeera.

However, he warned: “If Washington’s goal in sending this letter is to stir up discord, it would be yet another mistake to add to its previous ones.”

Araghchi played down talk of upcoming meetings between the two sides.

“What is being circulated in this regard is merely media speculation,” he said.

“We see no need to meet with the Americans at this stage. Our conditions are clear, and mediators are continuing their consultations regarding them,” he added.

Araghchi said whether Iran would hold direct or indirect talks with the US depended on Tehran’s conditions being met.

“Mediators have presented proposals concerning the nuclear dossier, which we are currently reviewing as part of the second phase,” he said.

“Qatari and Pakistani mediators are continuing consultations regarding our conditions,” he said.

Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, told Al Jazeera that any progress in Friday’s talks in Tehran was most likely on “the sequencing of the first steps needed to establish the barest of trust – without which further bolder steps are not possible”.

Araghchi said talks with Qatari mediators had shortened the time needed to implement Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

“The Qatari side proposed shortening the implementation period of the Iranian proposal to five days. We have reached a proposal at this stage that reduces the implementation period to two days,” he said.

“Our conditions include lifting the sanctions imposed following the Islamabad memorandum and reducing US forces in the region,” he said, adding, “We demand the restoration of oil waivers and the release of all our frozen funds, including those held in Qatar.”

Iran is also demanding recognition of shipping routes through the strait that it had discussed with Oman, and the closure of other routes, he said.

Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar Atas, reporting from Tehran, said there was “no remarkable flexibility in Iran’s position”, with Tehran insisting on the same demands while negotiations continue.

Under a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between the US and Iran in June, Washington guaranteed the oil waivers and said there would be no further restrictions on Iranian oil exports, Atas said. But when the MoU collapsed months later, the US cancelled all the waivers.

Tehran is also still insisting on the release of its frozen assets, including $6bn held in Qatar, and on the lifting of sanctions, not only those on its energy and nuclear file, but also those imposed since the MoU collapsed, which are putting huge pressure on Iran’s economy, he said.

The US, for its part, wants Iran to reopen the strait, and both sides want their demands met on the ground, not only on paper, Atas added.

In his remarks to Al Jazeera, Araghchi said his country does not rule out the possibility of an attack against Iran.

“We are prepared for all scenarios,” he said. “We have upgraded our weaponry, addressed our vulnerabilities, and tested new arms. Our forces are at the highest level of readiness.”

This comes as Iran’s armed forces chief of staff, Major-General Ali Abdollahi, said in a statement on Saturday that Iran would respond to any attack with “immense force”, with no geographical limits, and that it would decide when any new war ends.

Abdollahi said Iran was acting on Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei’s orders .

“We have a new stockpile of enemy targets and assets, and they are on our agenda,” he said. “America and Israel will face an unimaginable response, and we are the ones who will determine the end of any new war.”

⁠US ⁠Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a press conference on Saturday that President Donald Trump has not yet made ⁠a decision on whether to ⁠resume military action against Iran. He added that he did not know whether there was a specific timeframe ⁠for Qatar-led talks ⁠aimed at resolving hostilities.

Abbas Khamayar, a former Iranian diplomat, told Al Jazeera he expects the current situation to hold until next week’s US midterm elections .

articles.body:
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei issued a stark message on Friday, warning the U.S. against its reported plans to resume strikes against the country following the midterm elections.

Khamenei directed senior Iranian military officials in a meeting to deliver an “immediate, impactful response without geographical limitations,” according to Iran’s official IRNA news agency .

The leader reportedly instructed these military leaders to update their target database “to ensure that all physical and non-physical assets” of the U.S. and Israeli armies are brought within reach of the Iranian armed forces.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

On Friday, several outlets reported that the U.S. had notified several Arab countries to prepare for a short U.S. military campaign following the Nov. 3 elections, with fresh attacks expected as soon as the following day, three senior Gulf Arab officials told MS NOW.

President Trump promised earlier this month he would not launch strikes against Iran ahead of the midterms, as he continues to face pressure to wind down this war amid rising energy prices and other costs tied to the conflict.

The war, which began with joint U.S.-Israeli strikes launched on Feb. 28, has now stretched over eight months. The conflict has cost the U.S. around $47 billion , according to an Oct. 16 estimate from U.S. Central Command.

At a rally last week , the president indicated his administration “may do another little Epic Fury” if Iran refuses to meet U.S. demands, in reference to the U.S.’s military operations against Tehran, dubbed “Operation Epic Fury.”

“If they’re smart, they’ll just say, ‘Let’s get down to business,’” the president said. “But, you know, I doubt they’ll do that because perhaps they’re not smart.”

The Trump administration has also waged a massive effort to isolate Iran’s economy, called “Operation Economic Outcast,” by placing sanctions on Iranian oil and imposing a U.S. naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil trading corridor.

The Treasury Department said in a Friday report that the campaign was “decimating” Iran’s economy, finding headline inflation in the country reached 90 percent in September.

articles.title: A California restaurant catered meals for a golfer's family at the Masters without agreeing on a price, then sent a $74,960 bill; after a $60,391 jury award, appeals judges upheld just $1,950 in extra fees
articles.summary: A family meal arrangement during one of golf's biggest tournaments turned into a costly legal dispute after a California restaurant sent a bill for nearly
articles.body: A family meal arrangement during one of golf's biggest tournaments turned into a costly legal dispute after a California restaurant sent a bill for nearly $75,000 without discussing the price beforehand. The restaurant had agreed to provide meals for a golfer's family and friends during the Masters tournament in Augusta, Georgia. However, after the family left two days early and received the invoice, it challenged the amount. The restaurant sued and won a jury award of $60,391, but its subsequent attempt to recover tens of thousands of dollars in additional legal fees and court reporting costs was largely rejected.In a judgment dated October 29, 2026, in Hanna Carroll Restaurant Group LLC v. Hagestad (G065313A), the California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Three, upheld a lower court's decision to award the restaurant only $1,950 in additional legal fees. According to the ruling available on Justia, the restaurant had requested $81,875 in legal fees and another $25,741.20 in court reporter costs. The appeals court found that it had not properly identified which legal expenses were specifically related to proving that a catering contract existed.How a catering arrangement turned into a disputeThe case involved Hanna Carroll Restaurant Group LLC, which operates a high-end restaurant in Orange County, California, and John Hagestad. In March 2022, Hagestad and his wife dined at the restaurant and were impressed with the food and service. They later contacted its chief operating officer, Dave Hanna, about arranging meals for their family and friends during the Masters golf tournament in April.Their son was competing at the tournament in Augusta, Georgia, and the family expected between 20 and 30 people at each meal. Dave Hanna sent them a proposed menu covering breakfast and dinner for seven days. The family approved the menu, but the two sides never signed a written contract or discussed the price of the catering services.During the tournament, the restaurant provided breakfast, dinner and a full bar for five days, serving an average of 25 guests per meal. The family unexpectedly left two days earlier than planned. After the event, the restaurant sent Hagestad an invoice for $74,960, which included a $5,000 discount. Hagestad disputed the amount, saying he would have made different arrangements had he known the final cost. In response, Dave Hanna withdrew the discount and added another $5,000 for the time and delay involved in seeking payment. This brought the bill to $84,960, which Hagestad refused to pay.Jury awards restaurant $60,391The restaurant subsequently filed a breach-of-contract lawsuit against Hagestad. During the legal proceedings, it asked him to admit that he had entered into a catering agreement covering all seven days of the Masters. Hagestad objected that the request was vague, ambiguous and contained multiple issues. However, he denied the entire request rather than admitting the parts he accepted and disputing the remaining details. The case went to trial, where Hagestad acknowledged that the restaurant had provided food and services during the tournament. However, he argued that their reasonable value was lower than the amount charged.The jury found in favour of the restaurant but awarded it $60,391, less than the original invoice. After the verdict, the restaurant sought $81,875 in cost-of-proof attorney fees under Section 2033.420 of the California Code of Civil Procedure. The provision allows parties to recover reasonable expenses when an opposing party unreasonably refuses to admit a fact that is subsequently proved during trial.Why the court limited additional legal feesThe restaurant argued that Hagestad should have admitted the existence of the catering agreement because emails between the two sides and the approved menu showed that they had agreed on the services. The appeals court agreed. It explained that even though the request for admission included several details that were not all established at trial, Hagestad had a duty to admit the portions that were true and deny only those he disputed.The judges also clarified that a contract does not necessarily need to specify a price if the amount can be determined objectively. Therefore, the absence of an agreed price did not automatically mean that no enforceable contract existed. However, the court rejected the restaurant's demand for the full $81,875. It had submitted all its legal fees incurred after Hagestad denied the request without separating the expenses related to proving the contract from those spent on other issues. Since the main issue at trial was the value of the catering services, proving that a contract existed had required relatively little time and effort. The appeals court found that the lower court had reasonably awarded only $1,950.Court rejects $25,741 in reporting costsThe restaurant also challenged the decision to strike its entire claim for $25,741.20 in court reporter costs. However, the appeals judges found that it had failed to provide sufficient evidence showing that the claimed transcript expenses were for transcripts ordered by the court or were otherwise recoverable under California law. It had also failed to produce the underlying invoices to establish the amount.In its October 29 ruling, the California Court of Appeal affirmed both lower court orders. It directed each side to bear its own costs of the appeal. The decision leaves the restaurant with its $60,391 jury award but no additional recovery beyond the $1,950 in legal fees. It also highlights the importance of clearly documenting contract terms and providing a proper breakdown of expenses when seeking reimbursement during litigation.You use AI every day. articles.body: With little transparency from Washington and warmongering from Tehran, people across the Middle East have been left anxious and confused, scanning for signals on whether the conflict between Iran and the United States will reignite. “The mood has definitely shifted,” a 36-year-old American national living in Saudi Arabia told CNN. She plans to leave before Tuesday’s midterms, after which US President Donald Trump has hinted renewed fighting is possible. “People are more cautious in general, and it feels like a waiting game to see what happens,” she added. At home and workplaces across Gulf Arab countries, questions are swirling. Residents are searching for clues that could help them make plans in case of school closures or travel disruption. The war began in February when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. It entered its eighth month this week with both sides still locked in a stubborn stalemate, neither making progress diplomatically nor capable of breaking the military impasse. Trump has offered little clarity on his endgame, oscillating between threats of further strikes and openness to possible diplomacy. Iran has tried to project its own deterrence, claiming it now possesses weaponry capable of striking more targets and inflicting even greater damage than before. Mediation is continuing – but a breakthrough would depend on at least one of the two sides breaching their own red lines. Trump wrote on social media earlier this month that Washington “will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections.” That the US president neither ruled out or confirmed strikes would resume afterwards is part of the reason for the ongoing nerves. “The US has been actively feeding into this regionwide sense of anxiety as it keeps signaling that another round of escalation might be imminent” Hasan Alhasan a senior fellow for Middle East policy at the International Institute for Strategic Studies told CNN. “But it’s becoming difficult to distinguish pressure tactics from genuine signals.” Adding to a sense that escalation could be imminent, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - who partnered the US in attacking Iran and has been pushing for new strikes - will remain in office despite losing his majority in the recent elections. Negotiations to form a new government in Israel look set to begin in earnest next week, but election results suggest it will be difficult for opposition parties to oust Netanyahu quickly, if at all. In the absence of clarity, residents in the region often rely on hearsay or search social media for reports on troop movements to determine whether a US strike is imminent. Over the past month, Iranian military commanders have also intensified a series of public messages claiming that Iran has built-up large stockpiles of new weapons, a tactic designed to induce fear among Washington’s allies in the region. A senior security official in Tehran told CNN that Iran will try to target infrastructure beyond oil facilities in the region, including AI, and warned that if the conflict resumes, it will be a long “war of surprises.” On Saturday, Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered a response “without geographical limitations” to any new threat, an apparent effort to present a leader still yet to be seen in public as playing an active role in military preparations. Foreign workers drawn to wealthy Gulf Arab states by economic opportunities and a tax-free lifestyle have for decades lived in relative stability in a region mired in conflict. That sense of security was shattered this year after the US and Israel launched the war, prompting Tehran to fire unprecedented barrages of ballistic missiles and drones onto Arab cities disrupting schools, travel and business and causing multiple casualties. Yet despite the war, many residents stayed put, telling CNN they feel confident under the protection of well-armed regional militaries. Practical concerns remain, though. “I’m actively trying not to think about that happening again because I really don’t want another winter with strikes,” Michelle, a 36-year-old American resident in Abu Dhabi told CNN. “I’ve always felt safe here…but I’m more concerned that our lives will have to change again.” This month, people were surprised to find out that families of US diplomats have begun discreetly leaving, with the sudden departures becoming known only after their children started saying goodbye to classmates at school. Many of those leaving had only recently returned to their posts after being ordered out at the height of the Iran war in March, making the exits feel like a frustrating and chaotic déjà vu. Fueling anxiety among residents are reports of thousands of US troops being dispatched to the region , as reported by the Associated Press. In Saudi Arabia, where major events have already been canceled and offices closed with staff working remotely after the Iran-allied Houthi rebels intensified strikes, residents told CNN the were concerned that a return to war could increase pressure on a country already embroiled in conflict along its southern border. “My neighbors and friends are bunkering for November but starting to get concerned about flights disruptions over the holidays,” said the 36-year-old American national in Saudi Arabia, comparing it to the covid era. “A lot of offices have moved to virtual or have reduced staff and remote learning is in place.” Elsewhere in the region, other international gatherings remain on track, though the risk remains that they could be disrupted if the US launches strikes in the coming week. In Abu Dhabi, where no attacks have been recorded since May, two US oil firms canceled plans for their executives to attend one of the region’s biggest oil conferences citing security concerns, Reuters reported. The event will proceed as scheduled next week with “strong” US participation and more than 120 American exhibiting companies, the organizer, DMG, told Reuters. The conference is expected to host nearly 240,000 people, according to the organizers. In Bahrain, one of the worst hit countries by Iran this year, people said they still felt the psychological impact of the war. “There is still that traumatic effect ,” 21-year-old Fawaz told CNN. “When you hear the bombings, it’s kind of like you feel it in your hearts and it’s hard to sleep at night, especially when there are bombings outside.” “A lot of people have become used to it by now but it’s still very scary,” he added. Time Out Despite growing anxiety over the possible resumption of war, there has been a flurry of quiet diplomacy over the past week. US Vice President JD Vance sent Iran’s top security official Mohsen Rezaei a letter, which the Islamic Republic is reviewing, according to Iranian media. Trump has claimed that the letter was related to an Iranian request for medical supplies, but it has raised hopes a diplomatic breakthrough could still be possible. Iranian officials are in Qatar for talks, a Qatari official said. Qatar has played a prominent role mediating, but the official added there was no US delegation present Saturday. In stark contrast to Trump’s warnings, the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack told CNN’s Becky Anderson that he thinks there could be “dramatic steps” in the next two weeks “We’re close. I think we’re very close to a place where we can finally say: Let’s just have a time out,” he said, adding that it is, however, a “matter of trust and who goes first.” On Saturday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he would not characterize if progress had been made in the talks over the past 48 hours, but claimed that “if there is a diplomatic solution, we would be open to it.” Asked by CNN if the Trump administration has any time frame for progress in the talks before it would resume military action, Rubio said, “I don’t know if there’s a time frame,” noting that “it’s up to the president to make decisions with regards to those sorts of things.” “There are multiple talks. Talks have actually never stopped. There’s been active conversations going, both in some cases directly, but often through intermediaries,” he said at a press conference in Atlanta. “The president’s preference in any challenge around the world is to try to solve it diplomatically and peacefully, if possible,” Rubio said. “He recognizes there are some issues in the world that cannot be solved peacefully, unfortunately, sadly, but we would prefer to solve it in that manner.” Rubio said that any diplomatic solution “can’t be one that endangers our national security or one that doesn’t meet our core concerns,” particularly around Iran’s nuclear program. Iranian officials have said they’re open for diplomacy with the US, but they do not have trust that talks will stop military strikes, citing several past occasions when the Islamic Republic was struck during negotiations. And a central figure also warned that Iran was not ready to compromise. “Iran’s conditions have been repeatedly and clearly stated to the mediators,” said Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the Iranian parliamentary speaker who is leading negotiations with the US. “The carrot-and-stick approach has no effect on Iran. Progress can only be achieved once Iran’s seven conditions have been agreed upon.”

articles.title: Americans voting from Mexico share a concern ahead of the midterms: the future of democracy
articles.summary: Americans living in Mexico say they are voting in the US midterm elections remotely to protect their country’s democracy amid political division back home.
articles.body: On the shores of Lake Chapala, in the Mexican state of Jalisco, lies one of the country’s most popular communities for American retirees. Between 8,000 and 10,000 foreign residents live in the lakeside town of Ajijic, and US politics remains part of everyday conversations, especially as the November 3 midterm elections approach. James Burns is one of those retired expats. Six years ago, he left Arizona to settle in this community, drawn by the warmth of its people. He says many Americans living here have already cast their ballots remotely, aware of what’s at stake. On November 3, all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats will be contested in elections that could change the balance of power in Washington. Regardless of who wins, what worries Burns is what may happen afterward, in a country he sees as increasingly polarized. “What comes next? We’ve seen how the situation in the United States has deteriorated, and frankly, we’re concerned that there could be violence, as well as about the safety of our family and friends,” he told CNN. Supporting democracy from afar From Mexico, thousands of Americans are closely following the issues on the ballot, including trade and tariffs, as well as the tightening of immigration measures and operations by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). These issues have divided Americans of all ages, at home and abroad. In Mexico City, 45-year-old Samuel McCree watches the political tensions gripping his country with worry and believes that defending its democratic institutions is more important than ever. “For a long time, we have taken our democracy for granted. That is why I believe that now, more than ever, we must support and protect it,” he told CNN. McCree settled in the Mexican capital after leaving Salt Lake City, Utah, two years ago. He grew up in a politically active family. His mother, Peg, is a member of the League of Women Voters, a nonpartisan civic organization founded in 1920, the same year the US ratified a constitutional amendment recognizing women’s right to vote. That family influence shaped McCree, who believes it is essential to continue participating in his country’s political decisions, even from abroad. Obstacles to voting Back in Ajijic, Burns says that while most expats like him prioritize the importance of voting, casting a ballot from Mexico can be complicated. Voters have to follow procedures that vary depending on the US state where they’re registered. That is why organizations such as Vote From Abroad have helped Americans in the region update their registrations, request their ballots and understand the requirements for returning them correctly. “They helped us make sure our voter registration was up to date and explained how to obtain our ballot and what we had to do to comply with each state’s small and peculiar election rules so that our votes would be counted,” Burns said. Another obstacle to voting remotely is the postal service. In Mexico City, McCree says sending a package to the US can be expensive and difficult, in part because Mexico’s postal service can be “somewhat unreliable.” To avoid possible delays, McCree gave his ballot to a friend who visited him in Mexico so they would take it to the US and mail it in. “I really wanted to make sure my ballot arrived on time so that my vote would be counted. And for me, as an American, it is very important to continue participating in the United States political process,” he told CNN. Despite such efforts, voter turnout among Americans living outside their country remains historically low, particularly in midterm elections. In 2022 there were approximately 91,000 voting-age US citizens residing in Mexico, according to the Federal Voting Assistance Program of the US Department of Defense, but only an estimated 3.1% of eligible voters participated in the midterms that year. Adding to the logistical difficulties is a legal controversy that has raised new concerns about the rules for voting from abroad. The Trump administration has changed part of the federal form that citizens use to vote from another country, removing the option that allowed them to identify as US citizens who have never resided in the United States. That category includes people born abroad to US citizens who may have the right to vote under the laws of certain states. The Democratic National Committee has filed a lawsuit against the Defense Department and the Office of Management and Budget over the change, arguing that it could make it harder for voters to register and request ballots. Tension and distrust Although the controversy affects a specific group of voters, it is unfolding amid a broader debate over access to the ballot and election rules. It is an issue that concerns Bradley Narduzzi, who has been voting from Mexico for two decades and says he has never before felt so much uncertainty about the process. “There has never been a situation where you have to worry about your vote. This is the first time in my life — I’m in my 50s — that I’ve been worried about my vote. It’s alarming,” Narduzzi warns. Political polarization, questions about election rules and the debate over election integrity have contributed to distrust among some segments of the US electorate. Although Narduzzi says he still trusts his country’s electoral system, he acknowledges that not everyone shares that confidence. As a visual artist, Narduzzi travels frequently to Texas, where he says he has noticed people becoming more cautious, even when expressing their opinions. “But it’s alarming. And many people are watching what’s happening. They are very careful about what they do, what they say and what they write,” he says with concern. Immigration is another issue that, according to Narduzzi, has contributed to this climate of tension. Deportation policies, border control measures and the role of immigration authorities have dominated part of the US political debate, and are also spilling over into private conversations. “We have a major immigration problem. So that is also a cause for concern. And yes, I think we all know that we are going through a tense moment. We live in tense times,” he says.

articles.title: Mexico comes alive during annual Day of the Dead celebrations
articles.summary: Bright orange marigolds, glowing candles and faces painted like the elegant skeletons known as catrinas fill the streets of Mexico every year during the country’s Day of the Dead celebrations.
articles.body: MEXICO CITY — Bright orange marigolds, glowing candles and faces painted like the elegant skeletons known as catrinas fill the streets of Mexico every year during the country’s Day of the Dead celebrations. Festivities begin in October and lead up to Nov. 1 and 2, when the souls of deceased loved ones are believed to temporarily return to earth to reunite with their families. No one knows when the first observance took place, but it is rooted in agriculture-related beliefs from Mexico’s pre-Hispanic era. Catholic traditions were incorporated into the celebration after the Spanish conquest in 1521. Today, celebrations are marked by massive parades running along Mexico City’s main avenue. Streets, businesses and markets are cloaked in orange Mexican marigold flowers, or cempasuchil, believed to light the path of the dead back to earth with their bright colors. Traditional pan de muerto, or bread of the dead, lines the display cases of bakeries. Families decorate altars to their loved ones in their homes, placing treats, food and mezcal as offerings next to photos of their loved ones. On the night of Nov. 1, families gather at cemeteries across the country to reconnect with their dead just as their ancestors have done for centuries. But as the tradition and the Mexican capital have increasingly gained an international spotlight, and states like Oaxaca and Michoacan have seen an influx of tourists, some regions have experienced tensions around overtourism. In Mexico City, many locals are skeptical of an annual parade featuring floats decorated with catrinas. The procession was created for the 2015 James Bond film “Spectre” and later incorporated into the city’s celebrations, though it was not previously part of the tradition. In Janitzio, a small island on a lake in the central state of Michoacan, where celebrations were recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008, authorities closed the pantheon to tourists for the first time this year. The closure came after the island’s community council reported the collapse of damaged tombs, crosses and parts of the cemetery’s perimeter wall because of the flood of people. Only local families and friends of those buried there would be allowed in.

articles.title: Evacuees from Russia-controlled Oleshky arrive back in Ukraine amid U.S.-brokered ceasefire
articles.summary: Residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky arrived back in Ukraine on Saturday amid a localized U.S.-brokered ceasefire agreement. The halt in fighting, which was secured earlier this month by first lady Melania Trump, went into effect on Tuesday and is set to last through Saturday. Residents were given the choice of being transported…
articles.body:
Residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky arrived back in Ukraine on Saturday amid a localized U.S.-brokered ceasefire agreement .

The halt in fighting, which was secured earlier this month by first lady Melania Trump, went into effect on Tuesday and is set to last through Saturday.

Residents were given the choice of being transported to Russia, Ukraine or remaining in the city with replenished food supplies. Those who chose to return to Ukraine were transported through Russia and Belarus before reaching the country’s Chernihiv region on Saturday.

The city, which is located in the Russian-controlled Kherson region, has faced shortages in food, medicine and other vital supplies amid the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war . Around 2,000 people were reportedly trapped in the city, including a large elderly population.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky thanked the first lady for her efforts to secure the localized ceasefire in a Saturday social media post announcing the return of the Oleshky evacuees to Ukraine.

“As of now, Ukrainian citizens from Oleshky have crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv region,” he wrote. “All of them will receive the assistance they need. It is important that government agencies and all the regional and local authorities involved work effectively and help our people adapt.”

Zelensky expressed his hope that humanitarian access to the city would “remain open.”

Melania Trump responded on social media Saturday to a video shared by a Ukrainian official of the moment the residents reached Ukraine.

“Oleshky proves we can raise humanity above war,” she wrote. “Together, we can build a peaceful planet, a world of promise for our children.”

On Friday, the first lady said the humanitarian convoy effort, which included 25 buses and 50 medical professionals, could safely evacuate 750 people from the city.

“All elements of the convoy, including the safe passageway in and out of Oleshky, was established through mutual agreement between Russian and Ukrainian leaders,” she wrote in a social media post .

José Andrés, the founder of World Central Kitchen, said his nonprofit team had set up food supplies in preparation for the evacuees’ arrival back in Ukraine.

“The route was long: from Oleshky through Crimea to Anapa in Russia, then a flight to Belarus and onward by road into Chernihiv region. After a journey like that, warm, good food matters a great deal,” Andrés wrote on social media , alongside a video of evacuees going through a food line.

Zelensky praised the nonprofit’s assistance and said he was “proud and grateful” for Andrés’s involvement in this effort.

“Thank you to you and the entire World Central Kitchen team for the warmth of your dishes and hearts,” the Ukrainian leader wrote in a social media post .

images.caption: Residents of Oleshky react after being evacuated from their Russian-occupied hometown as they cross the Belarus-Ukraine border in Chernyhiv region, Ukraine, Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky)

articles.title: Cyclone Arnab brings surplus Oct rains to 10 districts in Andhra, cuts statewide deficit from 47% to 18%
articles.summary: Cyclone Arnab brought heavy Oct 2026 rains to 10 Andhra Pradesh districts, cutting the state rainfall deficit from 47% to 18%; Srikakulam saw 99% surplus.
articles.body: Visakhapatnam: Around ten districts in Andhra Pradesh recorded the wettest Oct 2026, with parts of the state receiving heavy to extremely heavy rainfall due to the cyclone Arnab. Srikakulam district in north AP recorded more than 90% surplus rainfall in Oct and the rains have led to floods in parts of the district.The cumulative rainfall figures across the state from Oct 1 to Oct 30 stand at 128.1 mm against a normal of 155.7 mm, which is around 18% deficit. The coastal AP — 19 districts and Yanam of Puducherry — region in the state recorded 157.2 mm of rainfall against a normal of 175.1 mm, which is 10% deficit, while the Rayalaseema (nine districts) region in the state recorded 94.4 mm of rainfall against a normal of 128.1 mm, which is around 26% deficit in Oct.The state recorded rainfall of 71.6 mm as against 134.5 mm from Oct 1 to 26 (around 47% deficit). Rainfall due to cyclone Arnab has reduced the state’s average rainfall deficit from 47% (on Oct 26) to 18% (on Oct 30).Among all the districts in the state, Srikakulam district recorded 401.9 mm of rainfall from Oct 1 to 30, which is around 99% surplus over the normal rainfall of 201.5 mm, followed by 89% surplus rainfall in Vizianagaram, 51% surplus rainfall in Anakapalle, 44% surplus rainfall in Vizag, 39% surplus each in Dr BR Ambedkar Konaseema and Kakinada districts, 28% surplus in Guntur and 21% surplus in ASR district. In Rayalaseema region, Chittoor and Tirupati districts recorded 30% and 20% surplus rainfall in Oct.Mrutyunjay Mohapatra, the director general (meteorology) of India Meteorological Department (IMD), said IMD forecast subdued rainfall activity in Andhra Pradesh in Oct 2026, but the heavy to extreme rainfall activity in Andhra Pradesh in the last week of October was the result of the severe cyclonic storm Arnab.
